content.overview: Harvest readiness is a representative biological and quality decision. Maturity can vary across canopy position, flower age and genotype, so one top flower, one calendar date or one universal trichome-color threshold is not enough.

vocabulary.definition: Observation of multiple meaningful flower positions selected to characterize crop developmental state.
Variation in developmental condition across flowers, positions or plants in the same crop.
Defined production or quality goal used with maturity evidence to support timing decisions.

sections.title: Sample across meaningful positions
sections.body: Top, interior and lower flowers can differ in developmental state. A representative plan is stronger than convenience sampling from the most mature-looking site.

sections.title: Use multiple maturity cues
sections.body: Morphology, trichome observations and crop history can contribute to readiness, but each has limits. The decision should preserve the context and sampling method.

sections.title: Avoid universal visual percentages
sections.body: Research supports developmental relationships under studied conditions but does not justify one amber percentage or stigma percentage for every cultivar and quality objective.

workedExamples: A top flower looks substantially more mature than lower/interior flowers; the correct response is broader representative sampling, not declaring the whole lot ready from the top sample.
commonMistakes: Using one flower to represent the crop.
Treating one visual threshold as universal.
content.practicalApplication: Create a harvest-readiness sampling plan with positions, observations, crop objective, limitations and the evidence needed before release to harvest.
content.summary: Harvest readiness depends on representative maturity evidence and stated quality objectives, not one convenient visual cue.
